Discussion Summary of main results This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours. Altogether, we identified 10 studies for inclusion in this review. Most studies included adults with malignant solid tumours of different types. Of these, three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster, five studies (one RCT and four controlled NRSIs; 76,372 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza, and one RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19. The RCTs assessing herpes zoster and COVID‐19 vaccines were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines. We assessed the RCTs as being at low or moderate risk of bias, while we judged most of the controlled NRSIs to be at critical risk of bias, primarily due to concerns about confounding. Further, we identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine and one controlled NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines. We also identified one completed but not yet published study, and 11 studies await classification due to unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest, results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination. We did not identify RCTs or controlled NRSIs on vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. In the following, only the results from RCTs are presented. Results from controlled NRSIs are detailed in the Effects of interventions section of the main text. Effects of interventions Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 1 . Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster probably make little or no difference in all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster make little or no difference in adverse events (any grade) up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence) and probably make little or no difference in serious adverse events up to 30 days (moderate certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster may have little or no difference in the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after the final dose (low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 2 . We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on all‐cause mortality up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza in adverse events (any grade) up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on serious adverse events up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 3 . Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in participants without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably increase the number of participants with adverse events (any grade) up to 6 months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 may make little or no difference in the number of participants with serious adverse events up to 6 months after the second dose (low‐certainty evidence). Overall completeness and applicability of evidence The evidence summarised in this systematic review applies to vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster, influenza, and COVID‐19 in adults with solid tumours. The findings are particularly relevant for healthcare providers involved in the care of these people, as they can guide vaccination strategies aimed at reducing infection risk. Understanding vaccine efficacy and safety is crucial for adults with solid tumours when making informed health decisions. The review indicates that certain vaccines, specifically those for herpes zoster and COVID‐19, demonstrate high‐ or moderate‐certainty evidence for reducing infection incidence. However, these vaccines may be associated with localised events at the injection site or any‐grade adverse events. It is important to note that the applicability of these findings may vary based on specific types of malignancy and their stages. Additionally, cancer therapies can significantly impact immune function and vaccine efficacy. However, due to insufficient data, we could not determine whether there are differences in outcomes between various malignancies or cancer therapies. The RCTs on herpes zoster included adults with diverse solid tumour types, such as breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and lung cancer ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), all receiving chemotherapy. This diversity allows for some comparison regarding how chemotherapy impacts vaccine efficacy across different cancers. Additionally, there are variations in vaccine types used in these studies. In Mullane 2013 , participants received a heat‐treated zoster vaccine, while Mullane 2019 administered an inactivated varicella‐zoster virus vaccine. In contrast, Vink 2019 employed an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine. A distinction in vaccine types may be important because different formulations can elicit varying immune responses, which may impact their effectiveness. In contrast to the herpes zoster vaccines, the RCT on influenza vaccines focused on adults with neck and oesophageal cancers undergoing surgery ( Goldmann 2015 ). This may limit the generalisability of the findings to other cancer types or treatment modalities, since participants were vaccinated prior to surgery. While there is very low certainty in the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of influenza vaccination for this particular subset of patients, it may not directly apply to those receiving immunotherapy or other surgical interventions. To supplement our findings from Goldmann 2015 , which was published as correspondence, we incorporated data from controlled NRSIs. For instance, INVIDIa‐2 and Amdisen 2024 reported on the incidence of influenza across a wider range of cancers, including participants undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy or chemotherapy. However, the studies primarily focused on severe disease and may not capture milder cases or asymptomatic infections, which are also important for assessing vaccine efficacy. In contrast, the data from controlled NRSI suggests that there is an effect on all‐cause mortality (moderate‐certainty) ( Gögenur 2021 ). This difference may arise from the different populations and the timing of the vaccination analysed in the included studies. Gögenur 2021 focuses on post‐surgery vaccination across multiple cancer types scheduled for surgery. The timing of the vaccination was within 30 days post‐surgery. The study measured all‐cause mortality as an outcome 180 days to three years post‐surgery. Nevertheless, this long‐term follow‐up provides insights into the potential impact of post‐surgery influenza vaccination on survival outcomes, thereby enhancing the completeness of results. However, while this study increases applicability by addressing diverse patient populations, it is essential to consider that factors influencing mortality may be multifactorial and not solely attributable to vaccination status. With respect to any‐grade adverse events, there remains uncertainty regarding the effects of influenza vaccines as indicated by both RCT ( Goldmann 2015 ) and controlled NRSI ( Wijn 2018 ) data. Wijn 2018 focused on adults with lung cancer receiving nivolumab. The study provides insights into the interactions between seasonal influenza vaccination and immunotherapy, but their targeted nature may restrict generalisability to other cancer treatments or patient populations not undergoing similar therapies. Influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and new strains can emerge. Influenza vaccines are adjusted annually to ensure better efficacy against the currently circulating strains ( WHO 2024 ). Therefore, it is important to interpret our findings on influenza vaccines with caution, as the included studies cover various influenza seasons. For example, the study by INVIDIa‐2 focuses on the 2019/2020 influenza season, while Wijn 2018 investigates the 2015/2016 and 2016/2017 seasons and Amdisen 2024 covers the seasons 2007/2008 to 2017/2018. Gögenur 2021 recruited participants between 2010 and 2015, and Goldmann 2015 covers the period from 2005 to 2008. This variability means that studies conducted across different seasons may yield results that are not directly comparable or applicable to current strains circulating within specific populations. In terms of COVID‐19 vaccines, Thomas 2022 focused on adults with various solid tumours, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, but did not provide clear information about specific cancer treatments received by the participants. We used data from a mixed population of solid tumours and haematological malignancies for adverse events and serious adverse events analyses since we expect similar events across both groups ( Copeland 2024 ; Javadinia 2022 ). Based on the RCT data, COVID‐19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 (moderate‐certainty). As the data only originates from a post‐hoc subgroup analysis, we supplemented our findings with data from controlled NRSIs. In contrast, controlled NRSI data presents uncertainty regarding their effects. The controlled NRSI by Zhao 2024 , specifically examined adults with hepatocellular carcinoma, a group facing unique immunological challenges due to liver dysfunction and underlying viral infections (e.g. hepatitis), which could influence vaccine efficacy differently than in other solid tumours ( Sachdeva 2015 ). Moreover, differences in vaccination regimens complicate comparisons. Thomas 2022 used the BNT162b2 vaccine, while Zhao 2024 , included multiple vaccines such as CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Zifivax, Convidecia, and BNT162b2. Notably, in Zhao 2024 , a small proportion of participants (6.5%) were not fully vaccinated. Such an incomplete vaccination status could lead to underestimating the potential protective effect of vaccination against infection. Furthermore, Thomas 2022 recruited participants between July 2020 to January 2021. Based on the recruitment period, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta and gamma. In contrast, Zhao 2024 recruited participants between January 2022 and October 2022 where omicron was prevalent. The evidence is only applicable to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants prevalent at the time of the studies. It is also crucial for consumers and caregivers to be aware of the limitations regarding other vaccines due to insufficient data. Although there is a lack of evidence or only low to very low‐certainty evidence for many of the vaccines we were interested in for this particular group of adults with solid tumours, studies involving immunocompetent adults generally demonstrate that vaccines are well tolerated and effective in preventing severe outcomes and providing protection ( Demicheli 2018 ; Graña 2022 ; Plosker 2015 ). Due to the small number of included studies and lack of subgroup data in the primary studies, we were unable to adequately investigate the influence of effect modifiers, such as type of malignancy or treatment, through subgroup analyses. While most studies measure immunogenicity parameters such as antibody levels, seroconversion, or T‐cell responses, there are no correlates of protection defined. These surrogate endpoints are not considered as patient‐relevant outcomes. In this review, we focused only on patient‐relevant outcomes that we determined in a workshop conducted with people with cancer and their representatives. The involvement of adults with cancer and their representatives was essential to obtain a better understanding of patient‐important outcomes, to ensure a patient‐relevant focus for this systematic review, and to ensure that our findings remain relevant to consumers navigating complex healthcare decisions. Notably, none of the included studies measured quality of life. The studies included in our review were predominantly conducted in high‐income countries, which may not fully represent the challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). According to Kamboj 2024 , the availability, accessibility, and utilisation of vaccines amongst adults with cancer in LMICs present significant hurdles. Limited resources and infrastructure, along with logistical barriers, often hinder vaccine distribution in these regions. Additionally, the high cost of vaccines can render them financially unattainable for many individuals. Consequently, the lack of access to vaccines leaves individuals with cancer in LMICs vulnerable to serious infections, which can adversely impact their health outcomes. Our review identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one controlled NRSI ( NCT05774171 ) evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines, which may provide further insights into vaccine efficacy once they are completed. One RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine has been completed, but no results have been published yet ( NCT02998736 ). We further categorised 12 studies with unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest or results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination as 'awaiting classification' ( Bettinger 2022 ; EPIVAC ; Hayashi 2023 ; Kazemain 2023 ; Khaddour 2022 ; Klastersky 1986 ; Lau 2022 ; Leuva 2022 ; NCT01698177 ; NL‐OMON32477 ; Serrano 2022 ; Vinograd 2013 ). EPIVAC , a comprehensive population‐based cohort study, assessed the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines and provided data categorised for individuals with compromised immune systems. These encompass solid tumours, haematological malignancies, chronic severe nephropathy, asplenia, immunodeficiency (including HIV), and long‐term corticosteroid therapy or other immunosuppressive drugs. Since the data for these conditions were not analysed separately, we were unable to include the study. We will consider including these studies in an update of this review once results or sufficient information is available. Furthermore, we excluded numerous controlled NRSIs in which healthy individuals were used as a control group (e.g. Gomez 2021 ; Silveira 2019 ). Quality of the evidence Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from three RCTs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as high to low (see Table 1 ). We have high certainty in the evidence for the outcomes of incidence of herpes zoster, adverse events of any grade, and localised events at the injection site, and moderate certainty for the outcomes of all‐cause mortality and serious adverse events. Our main concern was imprecision due to wide confidence intervals. We have low certainty in the identified evidence for systemic events. We downgraded the certainty of the evidence for imprecision due to a wide confidence interval and inconsistency due to substantial statistical heterogeneity. Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT and four controlled NRSIs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low (see Table 2 ). For the RCT, we rated the certainty of the evidence as very low. Our main concerns were the risk of bias due to missing information on allocation concealment, missing data, selection of the reported results, and imprecision due to very wide confidence intervals, low number of participants, and low number of events (all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, and serious adverse events). For controlled NRSIs, we rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low. We downgraded the evidence for risk of bias due to confounding (incidence of influenza, all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade) and imprecision due to wide confidence intervals (incidence of influenza, adverse events of any grade). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to low (see Table 3 ). Our main concerns were imprecision due to a low number of events or wide confidence intervals (incidence of COVID‐19, serious adverse events), or indirectness due to a mixed population including participants with solid tumours and haematological malignancies (any‐grade adverse events and serious adverse events). Potential biases in the review process We followed the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to minimise several potential biases in the review process ( Higgins 2024a ). An experienced information specialist (IM) developed the peer‐reviewed search strategy. The sensitive search included relevant electronic databases, as well as clinical trial registries, to ensure comprehensive coverage of available literature. To uphold the integrity and reliability of our review process, we conducted a comprehensive search for errata and retractions related to the studies included in our analysis. This step was essential for identifying potential biases arising from flawed or retracted research that could impact our conclusions. To supplement the lack of RCTs, we performed searches for controlled NRSIs when no RCTs were available for vaccines targeting specific infectious diseases. This also included vaccines to prevent influenza and COVID‐19, as the identified RCTs were published as correspondence ( Goldmann 2015 ) or reported data on solid tumour participants in a post hoc subgroup analysis ( Thomas 2022 ). While correspondence and post hoc analyses might provide valuable insights, they are generally considered less informative compared to primary research articles. Due to the limitations of these publication types, we decided to search for controlled NRSI as well. Given the differences in study design and potential biases associated with controlled NRSIs, we did not pool data from RCTs and controlled NRSIs. In addition, we made a conscious decision to categorise eligible studies that did not report any relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification' rather than including or excluding them without having explored other ways to establish if our outcomes had been measured. This change reflects our commitment to ensuring that only studies with pertinent outcome data contribute to our findings. We included only studies with a minimum sample size of 20 participants per arm. This criterion was established to enhance the reliability and generalisability of our findings by ensuring that included studies had sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful effects. However, this inclusion criterion may also limit the number of available studies, potentially introducing bias if smaller but relevant studies are excluded from consideration (e.g. Chu 2013 ; Kumar 2012 ). In classifying interventions and outcomes, we based our decisions on the data available from the studies. We categorised the studies according to their design (RCTs versus controlled NRSIs) and focused on outcomes that were deemed important by adults with cancer and their representatives. Further, we distinguished between 'localised events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' as separate outcomes. Nonetheless, it is important to note that some studies reported symptoms such as headache or fever as single outcomes, which limited our ability to analyse these effects together ( Thomas 2022 ; Zhao 2024 ). In our analysis, we aimed to capture long‐term outcomes by using the longest available follow‐up data. However, this approach may present limitations, particularly due to variability in follow‐up durations across studies. Such differences may lead to inconsistencies in outcome reporting, introduce potential biases in assessing long‐term effects, and challenges in comparing results between studies with varying timeframes. In cases of missing data, if we needed more information, we contacted the study authors for additional data or relevant details. We received answers from the contact authors of three studies ( Amdisen 2024 ; Leuva 2022 ; Mullane 2013 ). However, we could not use the data from Leuva 2022 due to unclear follow‐up time after a full vaccination. The data from Amdisen 2024 were measured as incidence rates per 10,000 person‐years for the outcomes of incidence of influenza and all‐cause mortality. Due to the incompatible format of these outcomes, we only provide a narrative description, without assessing the risk of bias or certainty of the evidence. Given the small number of studies included in each comparison, the informative value of statistical methods for analysing publication bias, such as funnel plots, was limited. Moreover, due to the small number of included studies, we were unable to conduct any subgroup analyses that might have provided further insights into specific populations or intervention effects. Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews Notably, the ASCO guidelines addressed a research question similar to ours by systematically reviewing studies published between 2013 and 2023 ( Kamboj 2024 ). They focused on adults with solid tumours or haematological malignancies, including long‐term survivors and those who received haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, evaluating routine vaccines listed on the CDC immunisation schedules as well as travel vaccines. Their comparisons included placebo, different vaccines, or varying vaccination strategies. The outcomes assessed encompassed risk of infection, disease severity, mortality, immune responses, and vaccine safety ( Kamboj 2024 ). In terms of herpes zoster vaccines, Kamboj 2024 identified a study concerning solid tumours reporting adverse events ( Vink 2019 ), but did not include Mullane 2013 and Mullane 2019 as the guidelines focused on recombinant zoster vaccines (RZV). RZV, commonly known by its brand name Shingrix, is a recombinant form of glycoprotein E from the varicella‐zoster virus, which is a key protein involved in the virus's ability to infect cells ( Vink 2019 ). Our findings on herpes zoster vaccines align with those of a network meta‐analysis conducted by Xia 2022 , which reported that RZV demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo in immunocompromised individuals, achieving 60% efficacy (95% CI 49% to 69%). Adverse events associated with RZV were primarily related to injection site reactions and systemic effects, with no increased risk of serious adverse events or death. Kamboj 2024 indicated that "grade three solicited general adverse events" (i.e. moderate‐to‐severe adverse events actively monitored during the study), were reported by adults with cancer in both the vaccine and placebo arms but were more prevalent in the vaccine arms. This finding is consistent with our observations regarding the safety profile of herpes zoster vaccines. However, it is important to highlight that the analyses by Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 exclusively included studies assessing RZV, while our review encompassed studies assessing heat‐treated zoster vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). Additionally, Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 included studies across various immunocompromised conditions such as haematological malignancies, renal transplantation, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and HIV, alongside one study involving individuals with solid tumours ( Vink 2019 ), which was also part of our review. A previous Cochrane review on influenza vaccination conducted by Bitterman 2018 demonstrated that influenza vaccination is associated with reduced mortality and lower rates of infection‐related outcomes compared to non‐vaccination. This review encompassed a diverse population, including adults with solid tumours, haematological malignancies, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The inclusion of such a broad range of immunocompromised groups suggests that influenza vaccination may confer significant benefits across these populations. However, more recent systematic reviews have provided additional insights into the effects of influenza vaccination specifically in adults with cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. For instance, a systematic review by Tsiakos 2022 indicated that influenza vaccination appeared to have no effect on the mortality of adults with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Furthermore, it presented an acceptable safety profile, as it was not associated with an increased incidence of immune‐related adverse events, whether any grade or serious. In line with this, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 reported that vaccinated adults with cancer exhibited slightly lower rates of immune‐related adverse events compared to unvaccinated adults with cancer (32% versus 41%), reinforcing the notion that vaccination does not exacerbate safety concerns. Despite these findings, both reviews highlight the limitations in available data regarding other efficacy and safety outcomes. Tsiakos 2022 noted that limited data exist concerning progression‐free survival, humoral immunity response, cell‐mediated immunity response, and the incidence of influenza. Similarly, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 provided specific metrics indicating seroprotection rates for different influenza types (78% to 79% for type A and 75% for type B) but did not address these additional outcomes. However, most of the data are derived from observational retrospective studies with small sample sizes and unadjusted analyses ( Lopez‐Olivo 2022 ; Tsiakos 2022 ). The Cochrane review by Graña 2022 concluded that most COVID‐19 vaccines reduce or likely reduce the occurrence of confirmed symptomatic COVID‐19 when compared to placebo. For some vaccines, there is high‐certainty evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing severe or critical disease. Our findings align with this conclusion, as we also observed a reduction in the incidence of COVID‐19 amongst vaccinated participants without previous infection (moderate‐certainty evidence). Kamboj 2024 further reported numerous studies examining immunologic parameters related to COVID‐19 vaccination amongst adults with cancer. They identified five controlled NRSIs demonstrating reduced rates of hospitalisation and mortality or decreased COVID‐19 sequelae in vaccinated versus unvaccinated adults with cancer. However, these studies did not exclusively focus on adults with solid tumours but also included adults with haematological malignancies ( Kamboj 2024 ). This broader inclusion may account for some variability in outcomes, but it underscores the importance of vaccination across different cancer types. In terms of vaccine safety, our observations regarding adverse events are consistent with those reported by Javadinia 2022 , who noted that COVID‐19 vaccination in adults with cancer is generally well‐tolerated regardless of cancer type. Both systemic and local adverse events, including fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, asthenia, vomiting, headaches, muscle and joint pain, chills, transient lymphadenopathy, and injection site reactions, were reported across various studies. While Javadinia 2022 highlighted that most vaccine‐related side effects were grade two at most, they also pointed out the challenges posed by differing assessment methods across studies, which complicate meta‐analysis efforts, such as the lack of reporting on the exact prevalence of PCR‐confirmed COVID‐19 infections and their outcomes. Additionally, many studies included in their review lacked a control group or used healthy controls, complicating the analysis still further ( Javadinia 2022 ). Our review reveals notable gaps in the literature concerning other vaccines. Kamboj 2024 reported an absence of eligible studies for hepatitis B, tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines. This lack of data aligns with our findings regarding the limited research available on certain vaccinations for adults with solid tumours. Furthermore, Kamboj 2024 identified only one RCT that examined the timing of pneumococcal vaccination. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduce the incidence of herpes zoster (high‐certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site occur more frequently than with placebo or no vaccine (high‐certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether influenza vaccines affect all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, or serious adverse events (very‐low certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in adults without prior infection (moderate‐certainty evidence), but they probably increase adverse events of any grade (moderate‐certainty evidence). We found no randomised controlled trials or controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions that investigated the use of vaccines compared to placebo or no vaccine for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, in adults with solid tumours. Implications for research We have identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines ( NCT05774171 ). Additional research, preferably RCTs, is necessary to assess a wider range of available vaccines against infectious diseases such as pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, for which we did not identify any RCTs or prospective NRSIs. This lack of research limits our understanding of how these vaccines perform in adults with solid tumours. While we advocate conducting RCTs to obtain robust evidence, if such studies are not possible for ethical reasons, retrospective (matched) analyses of individuals with cancer who have or have not received the respective vaccination could provide some insights. Future studies should include individuals of various age groups and those with different types of solid tumours undergoing diverse treatments (such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy). This diversity is crucial, because different age groups may respond differently to vaccines due to variations in immune system function, and individuals with solid tumours may be undergoing treatments that affect their immune response. When investigating multiple malignancies, it is important to report results as subgroups. This approach allows researchers to identify specific populations that benefit most from vaccination and understand under which cancer therapies the vaccines may be less effective in preventing infection. Additionally, it needs to be investigated whether passive immunisation with monoclonal antibodies may offer more protection than vaccines for immunocompromised or immunosuppressed individuals. Research should not just focus on the usual immunological laboratory parameters, especially in populations where established correlates of protection are still lacking. The outcomes measured should be patient‐centred and important, such as the incidence of infection (tracking how often vaccinated individuals contract the targeted infectious disease), quality of life (assessing how vaccination impacts patients' overall well‐being and daily functioning), all‐cause mortality (evaluating whether vaccination correlates with mortality rates amongst individuals with solid tumours), and adverse events (monitoring any negative side effects resulting from vaccination). Additionally, studies should take into account periods when the risk of infection is heightened. For instance, during flu season (typically October to March), individuals with compromised immune systems may face increased risks. Future research should investigate potential effect modifiers that could influence the effectiveness of vaccines for preventing infectious diseases. These might include patient demographics (age, sex, comorbidities) and treatment modalities (type and timing of cancer therapies). Importantly, future research must also address the unique challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), where barriers such as limited healthcare infrastructure, vaccine availability, and socioeconomic factors can significantly impact vaccination efforts. By understanding how these characteristics impact vaccine efficacy in LMIC contexts, alongside other factors influencing outcomes in high‐income settings, healthcare providers can tailor vaccination strategies to individual patient needs more effectively. In summary, addressing these gaps through rigorous research will enhance our understanding of vaccine effects across diverse patient populations. By prioritising patient‐centred outcomes and considering various factors influencing vaccine efficacy, including those specific to LMICs, we can optimise vaccination strategies to improve health outcomes for individuals at risk for infectious diseases. between protocol and review Differences between the published protocol ( Bora 2023 ) and this full review are as follows. Title We made minor edits to the title in order to use UK spelling ('tumours') and Cochrane style, i.e. 'for preventing' rather than 'for the prevention of'. Objectives We changed the wording from "To assess the benefits and harms of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours" to "To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours." Type of interventions We changed the wording to "We included vaccines for the prevention of the following infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours" and listed the diseases of the vaccines they protect against instead of the pathogens to specify the diseases targeted by these vaccines. Types of outcome measures Instead of including studies regardless of the reported outcome data, we decided to categorise eligible studies that did not report any of the relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification'. We previously listed 'local events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' under the outcome 'adverse events of special interest'. As these were intended to represent two separate outcomes, we no longer summarise them under one bullet point in the review but list them separately. Selection of studies We used the Rayyan software ( Ouzzani 2016 ) instead of Covidence to screen the references. We listed excluded studies that initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, but that we later excluded, in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table, with the reasons for their exclusion, instead of listing all excluded studies. Search methods Although at least one RCT was identified for vaccines against influenza and COVID‐19, we searched for NRSIs, as the one RCT on influenza vaccines was published as correspondence only, and the one RCT on COVID‐19 reported on participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. To ensure the integrity and reliability of the studies included in this review, we searched for errata or retractions related to the included studies that may have been published on MEDLINE, Embase, or Retraction Watch. We did not contact experts in the field to retrieve information on unpublished studies. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information. Assessment of reporting bias As we did not pool the data in the meta‐analysis and included fewer than 10 studies per comparison, we did not generate funnel plots to assess reporting bias. Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity We removed the planned subgroup analysis based on duration of follow‐up (e.g. shorter versus longer follow‐up) because we grouped the measurement time points of eligible outcomes into short‐term (up to 12 weeks after full vaccination), medium‐term (from 12 weeks to 6 months after full vaccination) and long‐term (more than 6 months after full vaccination) observations, if sufficient data was available (see Types of outcome measures ). Due to the limited number of studies that provided relevant data for our critical outcome, we did not perform meta‐analysis and thus conducted no subgroup analysis. If heterogeneity was above 75%, we planned to explore this with subgroup and sensitivity analysis. Despite considerable heterogeneity in Analysis 1.5 , we decided to keep the pooled effect estimate, as the effects of the individual studies were clearly on one side. We were unable to conduct the planned sensitivity analyses because the risk of bias for these RCTs was classified as either 'low' or 'some concerns'. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We created the summary of findings tables manually and did not use GRADEpro GDT . We added a section on consumer involvement during protocol development. The order of the comparisons and summary of findings tables was prioritised by clinical experts, based on relevance to decision‐makers. If evidence from both RCTs and NRSIs was available for a single outcome, only the RCT data were presented in the summary of findings tables. documents.title: Efficacy and safety of seven Chinese patent medicines combined with conventional triple/quadruple therapy for <i>Helicobacter pylori</i>-positive peptic ulcers: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare the efficacy and safety of seven Chinese patent medicines (CPMs) combined with conventional triple/quadruple therapy (T/Q) for Helicobacter pylori-positive peptic ulcers.
DESIGN: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES: China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP database, Wanfang database, ScienceDirect, EBSCO, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and PubMed were searched through 1 June 2022.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) testing CPMs combined with T/Q for H. pylori-positive peptic ulcers were included. The CPMs included Anweiyang capsule, Jianweiyuyang tablets/capsule/granule, Jinghuaweikang capsule, Kangfuxin liquid, Puyuanhewei capsule, Weifuchun tablets/capsule and Weisu granule. At least one of the following outcome indicators was recorded: complete ulcer healing rate (CUHR), effective rate (ER), H. pylori eradication rate (HPER), rate of peptic ulcer recurrence (RPUR) and incidence of adverse reactions (IAR).
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Two researchers independently conducted the study selection and extracted data for included studies. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. A pairwise meta-analysis was performed using RevMan V.5.3. Network meta-analysis was performed using STATA/MP V.15.0. Confidence in the evidence was assessed using Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation.
RESULTS: A total of 36 RCTs involving 3620 patients were included. Compared with T/Q alone, Weisu+T/Q, Weifuchun+T/Q and Puyuanhewei+T/Q had the highest CUHR, ER and HPER, respectively. Weisu+T/Q and Jianweiyuyang+T/Q had the lowest RPUR and IAR, respectively. The cluster analysis results showed Jianweiyuyang+T/Q might be the best choice concerning efficacy and safety simultaneously, followed by Kangfuxin+T/Q.
CONCLUSION: Among the combination therapies with the CPMs, Jianweiyuyang+T/Q might be the most favourable option for H. pylori-positive peptic ulcers, followed by Kangfuxin+T/Q. Considering the limited quantity and quality of the included RCTs, the results should be interpreted with caution.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42022327687.
documents.conclusions:
Among the combination therapies with the CPMs, Jianweiyuyang+T/Q might be the most favourable option for H. pylori-positive peptic ulcers, followed by Kangfuxin+T/Q. Considering the limited quantity and quality of the included RCTs, the results should be interpreted with caution.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42022327687.

Abstract Objectives To compare the efficacy and safety of seven Chinese patent medicines (CPMs) combined with conventional triple/quadruple therapy (T/Q) for Helicobacter pylori -positive peptic ulcers. Design A systematic review and network meta-analysis. Eligibility criteria Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) testing CPMs combined with T/Q for H. pylori -positive peptic ulcers were included. The CPMs included Anweiyang capsule, Jianweiyuyang tablets/capsule/granule, Jinghuaweikang capsule, Kangfuxin liquid, Puyuanhewei capsule, Weifuchun tablets/capsule and Weisu granule. A pairwise meta-analysis was performed using RevMan V.5.3. Network meta-analysis was performed using STATA/MP V.15.0. Confidence in the evidence was assessed using Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Results A total of 36 RCTs involving 3620 patients were included. Compared with T/Q alone, Weisu+T/Q, Weifuchun+T/Q and Puyuanhewei+T/Q had the highest CUHR, ER and HP ER, respectively. Weisu+T/Q and Jianweiyuyang+T/Q had the lowest RPUR and IAR, respectively. Keywords: herbal medicine, complementary medicine, gastroduodenal disease, systematic review status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Series information Original research Received 2023 Mar 29; Accepted 2024 Apr 8; Collection date 2024. STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY The adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for network meta-analysis guidelines in the reporting of the study gave credence to the study methodology. Taking both efficacy and safety into account, cluster analysis was applied to evaluate the proper rank of the interventions because none of the combination therapies had an absolute advantage over the others. The confidence of evidence for the outcomes was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. The number of randomised controlled trials available in some comparisons was relatively small. Introduction Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) remains a notable health concern, as untreated cases may result in gastroduodenal perforation and bleeding. Helicobacter pylori ( HP ) infection is a key risk factor for PUD, disrupting the balance between mucosal defence mechanisms and aggressive factors. 1 The primary treatment for HP -positive PUD involves a combination of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and two antibiotics (triple therapy), or the addition of bismuth to create quadruple therapy. 2–4 The majority of triple and quadruple therapies demonstrated HP eradication rates of up to 70%, with a few regimens achieving rates surpassing 90%. 5 However, resistance to HP is progressively rising, 6 7 leading to increased complexity in the treatment of HP using conventional antibiotics. 8 Studies have indicated a high incidence of adverse reactions (IARs) associated with triple or quadruple therapy, particularly bismuth-containing quadruple therapy. 9 10 Consequently, the consideration of complementary therapeutic approaches is warranted in the management of HP -positive PUD. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has a long history in China, and some TCM materials have strong anti-HP effects, 11 12 can reduce gastric acid secretion and promote mucosa regeneration strongly. 13 Chinese patent medicines (CPMs), which are highly processed forms of TCM, offer advantages such as accessibility, ease of storage, portability and the elimination of the need for decoction. Recent studies have demonstrated the superior efficacy of oral CPMs combined with conventional triple/quadruple therapy (T/Q) in the treatment of HP -positive PUD, leading to their endorsement by guidelines 14 and expert consensus. 15 16 However, the comparisons of the various CPMs plus T/Q are still lacking. Network meta-analysis (NMA), an extension of pairwise meta‐analysis (PMA), is a statistical method that compares and ranks different treatments by combining direct and indirect comparisons. In this study, we conducted an NMA to compare and rank the seven CPMs combined with T/Q for treating HP -positive PUD to provide a basis for clinical decision-making. Methods The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD 42022327687) (see online supplemental file 1 : CRD42022327687.pdf). This manuscript was written following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for NMAs checklist 17 (see online supplemental file 2 ). Supplementary data bmjopen-2023-074188supp001.pdf Supplementary data bmjopen-2023-074188supp002.pdf Criteria for inclusion and exclusion Study type We confined our study design to randomised controlled trials (RCTs) published in Chinese and English. Non-randomised controlled studies, such as observational and laboratory studies, were excluded. Participants Patients diagnosed with HP -positive PUD were included. PUD was confirmed by gastroscopy. Diagnostic methods for detecting HP infection comprised urea breath testing, stool antigen testing, rapid urease testing and histological examination of gastric biopsies obtained during endoscopy. Serological testing for HP antibodies was not employed due to the inability of a positive result to definitively confirm an active infection without age, sex, race or region restriction. 2 3 18 Interventions The experimental groups were administered CPMs in combination with T/Q. The CPMs used in the study included Anweiyang capsule (AWY), Jianweiyuyang tablets/capsule/granule (JWYY), Jinghuaweikang capsule (JHWK), Kangfuxin liquid (KFX), Puyuanhewei capsule (PYHW), Weifuchun tablets/capsule (WFC), and Weisu granule (WS). Each CPM was considered as an individual intervention in the analysis. Controls The control group received treatment with T/Q. Following the fifth Chinese National Consensus Report on the Management of HP Infection 18 and the 2022 Chinese National Clinical Practice Guideline on HP Eradication Treatment, 19 quadruple therapy (two antibiotics+PPI+bismuth) is preferred over triple therapy (two antibiotics+PPI) for HP infection. However, recent findings from a NMA 20 indicate that not all quadruple therapy regimens are more effective than triple therapy for HP eradication. The American College of Gastroenterology Clinical Guideline also 4 suggests that certain triple therapy may be suitable for HP eradication. Consequently, both triple therapy and quadruple therapy were considered standard treatment plans in our study. The antibiotic regimen should be limited to a maximum duration of 2 weeks. 2 4 18 19 The triple or quadruple therapy should be identical in the experimental and control groups. Otherwise, the studies would be excluded. Outcomes measures At least one of the outcome indicators, such as complete ulcer healing rate (CUHR), effective rate (ER), HP eradication rate ( HP ER), recurrence rate (rate of peptic ulcer recurrence, RPUR) and IAR, must be documented. Three key points should be highlighted regarding these outcome measures. First, an effective response was characterised by a reduction of more than 50% in the ulcer area following the treatment. 21 Second, successful eradication of HP infection was confirmed through urea breath testing, stool antigen testing or rapid urease testing plus histological identification of HP (Giemsa staining), at least 4 weeks after discontinuation of medication. 2 4 18 Third, recurrence of peptic ulcer was assessed via gastroscopy 6–12 months post-therapy cessation. Literature searches We conducted a comprehensive search of relevant publications up to 1 June 2022 in Chinese-language and English-language databases such as the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP database, Wanfang database, ScienceDirect, EBSCO, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and PubMed. Our search strategy was tailored for each database, using a combination of Mesh, title, abstract, keywords or free-text words. The retrieval terms included Anweiyang, Jianweiyuyang, Jinghuaweikang, Kangfuxin, Puyuanhewei, Weifuchun, Weisu, HP, gastric ulcer, duodenal ulcer and peptic ulcers. The search strategy is available in online supplemental table S1 . All the records were concurrently collected and processed in NoteExpress software. Study selection and data extraction Two researchers (ZJ and BD) independently selected studies based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted using a preset data extraction form by BD and YQ Zhang. The information extracted encompassed vital publication details (name of the first author, year of publication), participant characteristics (sample size, age, sex, disease duration and ulcerated area or diameter), intervention specifics and outcome indicator data. Disagreements were resolved through discussions with a third researcher (ZY or YC). Quality of bias assessment of included studies The quality of the included studies was assessed according to the Cochrane risk of bias tool, 22 including the adequate method for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting and other biases. Two researchers (ZJ and YL) independently assessed the risk of bias, and any disagreement was resolved by discussion with a third researcher (ZY or YC). Data analysis Pairwise meta-analysis PMA was conducted using RevMan V.5.3 software. Relative risk (RR) with a 95% CI was calculated for the dichotomous outcomes. Heterogeneity among the included studies was evaluated using the I 2 statistic. Substantial heterogeneity, defined as I 2 statistics exceeding 50%, prompted the utilisation of the random-effects model for PMA, while the fixed-effects model was employed in other instances. Network meta-analysis The NMA was conducted using the network package in STATA/MP V.15.0, wherein the RR with a 95% CI for the dichotomous outcomes was calculated. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. The surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA) was calculated to rank each treatment. 23 The cluster analysis was used to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the interventions and determine the optimal CPMs. Additionally, the summary results of all pairwise comparisons and NMAs were presented in the league tables. Network plots were constructed to visualise the comparisons. Each node represented an intervention, and its size was weighted by the number of subjects in each intervention. The thickness of the connecting line represented the number of included studies. 23 If there were closed loops in the intervention structure, the inconsistency of the evidence should be assessed. 24 The 95% predictive interval (95% PI) was calculated to describe the heterogeneity in this NMA. Uncertainty stemming from heterogeneity was characterised by discrepancies between the 95% CIs and their corresponding 95% PI. 23 25 In instances of substantial heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses were performed by excluding potentially biased studies. Transitivity was examined by assessing the distributions of potential effect modifiers across comparisons. These effect modifiers encompassed the following items: age, disease duration, ulcerated area or diameter, duration of the antibiotic course, duration of the full therapeutic course and the case numbers of duodenal ulcer, gastric ulcer and compound ulcer. Additionally, publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot where a symmetrical funnel suggests little bias. Certainty of the evidence The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) was used to assess the confidence of evidence for the outcomes of the NMA. 26–28 The certainty of the NMA estimates was rated as ‘high’, ‘moderate’, ‘low’ or ‘very low’ based on considerations of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. Patient and public involvement Patients or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting, or dissemination plans of our research. Results Selection and identification of studies The literature search yielded a total of 2452 studies. As indicated in figure 1 , the full text of 393 references was screened after title and abstract screening. Ultimately, 36 two-armed RCTs 29–64 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the NMA. All studies were performed in China, and the publication years ranged from 2008 to 2022. Figure 1 A flow diagram of the literature screening and selection processes. CNKI, China National Knowledge Infrastructure; HP, Helicobacter pylori ; PU, peptic ulcer; RCT, randomised controlled trial; WFD, Wanfang database; WOS, Web of Science. Characteristics of included studies 36 RCTs 29–64 involving 3620 patients were included. 1830 patients received combination therapy (CPM+T/Q), and 1790 patients received T/Q alone. The duration of the full therapeutic course ranged from 2 to 8 weeks. Among the included studies, AWY, JHWK, JWYY, KFX, PYHW, WFC and WS were studied in 1, 10, 2, 16, 2, 2 and 3 trials, respectively. The characteristics of the 36 eligible RCTs are presented in online supplemental table S2 . The characterisations of the seven CPMs are presented in online supplemental table S3 . The summary of the outcomes data in the 35 included studies is presented in online supplemental table S4 . Risk of bias of included studies All of the included studies mentioned randomisation, with only 12 trials 31 38 39 50 52 54–57 59 61 63 providing detailed descriptions of their randomisation methods, which were categorised as ‘low risk’. The majority of RCTs were deemed to have an ‘unclear risk’ in terms of allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, selective reporting and other biases, due to inadequate information. However, two studies were found to have a high risk of bias related to blinding 29 63 as the duration of the full therapeutic course differed between the control and experimental groups, potentially leading to variation in the IARs. All outcomes were laboratory measurements in nineteen RCTs 30 32–35 37 40 42 43 47 49–53 58 60 61 64 and unlikely to be influenced by lack of blinding, indicating a low risk of bias for blinding in these studies. Additionally, the risk of bias for incomplete outcome data was low in 33 studies, with only 3 RCTs 49 55 59 classified as ‘high risk’ due to a high number of patients lost to follow-up. In terms of selective reporting, one RCT 48 was considered to have a ‘low risk’ as all five outcomes were reported. The risks of biases in the included studies are presented in online supplemental figure S1 and online supplemental figure S2 . Overall, most studies demonstrated a moderate risk of bias in the seven domains assessed. Results of the PMA We assessed the impact of CPMs on CUHR, ER, HP ER, RPUR and IAR. Compared with T/Q alone, AWY+T/Q (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.30), JHWK+T/Q (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.31), JWYY+T/Q (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.82), KFX+T/Q (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.39), PYHW+T/Q (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.19 to 2.77), WFC+T/Q (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.32) and WS+T/Q (RR 2.08, 95% CI 1.18 to 3.67) displayed significantly improved CUHR; KFX+T/Q (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.14) and WFC+T/Q (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.20) displayed significantly improved ER; JHWK+T/Q (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.21), JWYY+T/Q (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.70), KFX+T/Q (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.23) and PYHW+T/Q (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.04) displayed significantly improved HP ER; KFX+T/Q (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.53) and WS+T/Q (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.10, 0.67) significantly reduced RPUR (see online supplemental table S5 and online supplemental table S6 ). No significant difference was observed in any comparisons among the interventions in terms of IAR (see online supplemental table S5 and online supplemental table S7 ). In terms of ER, the results of the heterogeneity test indicated significant heterogeneity among the different interventions with I 2 values of 96% for JHWK+T/Q versus T/Q, I 2 values of 57% for WS+T/Q versus T/Q, necessitating the use of random-effects models. The other comparisons with I 2 <50% did not exhibit significant heterogeneity, necessitating the use of fixed-effects models (see online supplemental table S5 ). Results of the NMA Evidence network The network plots are presented in figure 2 . All the combined therapies of CPM plus T/Q had at least one comparison with T/Q alone while all of the combined therapies lacked a closed loop between them, indicating that inconsistency testing was unnecessary. Figure 2 Network plots of the outcomes. (A) complete ulcer healing rate; (B) effective rate; (C) HP eradication rate; (D) rate of peptic ulcer recurrence; (E) incidence of adverse reactions. HP, Helicobacter pylori . Complete ulcer healing rate 28 RCTs 29 33–52 55–57 59–61 63 with 8 interventions reported CUHR. AWY+T/Q (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.37), JHWK+T/Q (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.30), JWYY+T/Q (RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.83), KFX+T/Q (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.36), PYHW+T/Q (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.84) and WS+T/Q (RR 2.08, 95% CI 1.16 to 3.74) displayed significantly improved CUHR compared with T/Q alone. However, no significant difference was observed in any comparisons among the combined therapies (see figure 3A and online supplemental table S6 ). According to the SUCRA values, WS+T/Q ranked first for improving CUHR, followed by PYHW+T/Q and AWY+T/Q (see online supplemental table S8 ). Figure 3 Predictive interval plots of the outcomes. (A) Complete ulcer healing rate; (B) effective rate; (C) HP eradication rate; (D) rate of peptic ulcer recurrence; (E) incidence of adverse reactions. HP, Helicobacter pylori; RR, relative risk. Effective rate 28 RCTs 32–36 38–48 50 51 53–57 60–64 with 6 interventions reported ER. JHWK+T/Q (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.17), KFX+T/Q (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.14) and WFC+T/Q (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.25) displayed significantly improved ER compared with T/Q alone. No other comparisons revealed significant differences (see figure 3B and online supplemental table S6 ). According to the SUCRA values, WFC+T/Q ranked first for improving ER, followed by WS+T/Q, JHWK+T/Q and JWYY+T/Q (see online supplemental table S8 ). HP eradication rate 13 RCTs 30–32 35–38 40 48 51 52 57 58 with 5 interventions reported HP ER. JHWK+T/Q (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.18), JWYY+T/Q (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.70), KFX+T/Q (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.23) and PYHW+T/Q (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.04) displayed significantly improved HP ER compared with T/Q alone. However, no significant difference was observed in any comparisons among the combined therapies (see figure 3C and online supplemental table S6 ). According to the SUCRA values, PYHW+T/Q ranked first for improving HP ER, followed by JWYY+T/Q and KFX+T/Q (see online supplemental table S8 ). Rate of peptic ulcer recurrence 12 RCTs 29 43 44 47 48 51 52 55 56 59 63 64 with 5 interventions reported RPUR. KFX+T/Q (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.56) and WS+T/Q (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.69) significantly reduced RPUR compared with T/Q alone. No other comparisons revealed significant differences (see figure 3D and online supplemental table S6 ). According to the SUCRA values, WS+T/Q ranked first for reducing RPUR, followed by AWY+T/Q and KFX+T/Q (see online supplemental table S8 ). Incidence of adverse reactions 17 RCTs 29 31 36 38 39 41 44–46 48 54–57 59 62 63 with 7 interventions reported IAR. No significant difference was observed in any comparisons among the interventions (see figure 3E and online supplemental table S7 ). According to the SUCRA values, JWYY+T/Q ranked first for reducing IAR, followed by JHWK+T/Q and KFX+T/Q (see online supplemental table S8 ). Cluster analysis Cluster ranking considering both efficacy and safety was performed to simultaneously weigh the risks and benefits of each intervention. Each cluster was assigned a specific colour, with interventions located in the upper right corner deemed superior. The results of the cluster analysis, based on SUCRA values for IAR and CUHR (see figure 4A ), indicated that JWYY+T/Q was the most effective and safe intervention, followed by a cluster containing KFX+T/Q. This trend was also observed in the cluster analysis based on SUCRA values for IAR and ER (see figure 4B ), as well as SUCRA values for IAR and HP ER (see figure 4C ). KFX+T/Q was one of the best treatment strategies based on the cluster analysis results using SUCRA values for IAR and RPUR (see figure 4D ). In contrast, T/Q alone might be the worst treatment strategy considering the comprehensive rank of cluster analysis. Figure 4 Cluster analysis plots. (A) IAR (x-axis) and CUHR (y-axis); (B) IAR (x-axis) and ER (y-axis); (C) IAR (x-axis) and HP ER (y-axis); (D) IAR (x-axis) and RPUR (y-axis). AWY, Anweiyang capsule; CUHR, complete ulcer healing rate; ER, effective rate; HP ER, Helicobacter pylori eradication rate; IAR, incidence of adverse reactions; JHWK, Jinghuaweikang capsule; JWYY, Jianweiyuyang capsule/granule; KFX, Kangfuxin liquid; PYHW, Puyuanhewei capsule; RPUR, rate of peptic ulcer recurrence; T/Q, conventional triple or quadruple therapy; WFC, Weifuchun tablet; WS, Weisu granule. Heterogeneity check The heterogeneity test revealed that none of the comparisons involving RPUR and IAR was affected by the estimated heterogeneity, as indicated by consistent 95% CIs and respective 95% PIs (see figure 3D,E ), ensuring the stability of the estimations of NMA. Three of the 28 comparisons involving CUHR (see figure 3A ), 3 of the 15 comparisons involving ER (see figure 3B ) and 2 of the 10 comparisons involving HP ER (see figure 3C ) were influenced by estimated heterogeneity because their 95% CIs and respective 95% PIs were inconsistent. The estimate of heterogeneity tau 2 for the NMA of CUHR, ER and HP ER was 0.01, 0 and 0, respectively, suggesting low levels of heterogeneity and relatively stable estimations in the NMA. Funnel plot and publication bias The funnel plots are shown in online supplemental figure S3 . Scatters in the funnel plot for CUHR, HP ER, RPUR and IAR were almost visually symmetrical, suggesting low publication biases. However, the funnel plots for ER displayed a slightly asymmetrical distribution, hinting at the possibility of publication bias. Certainty of the evidence Online supplemental table S9 provides a summary of the certainty of evidence for the outcomes. The certainty of evidence was very low for all the comparisons among the combined therapies, due to study limitations (most information is from studies at unclear risk of bias, downgrade one level), indirectness and imprecision. The certainty of evidence was low for most of the direct comparisons between CPMs+T/Q and T/Q because of study limitations, inconsistency (due to heterogeneity) and imprecision. Regarding CUHR, HP ER and RPUR, there was moderate confidence in estimates supporting the use of CPMs+T/Q over T/Q alone. For example, the CPMs were JWYY, KFX and WS with respect to CUHR. Discussion PUD is a prevalent gastrointestinal disorder that poses a significant risk to human health. 65 TCMs, including CPMs, have been frequently used for the treatment of PUD. The PMA and NMA were conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the seven CPMs in combination with T/Q for the management of PUD. The results indicated that seven combination therapies (CPMs+T/Q) were notably more effective in improving CUHR, ER, HP ER or reducing RPUR compared with T/Q alone across at least one outcome measure. Furthermore, the ranking results demonstrated that T/Q alone consistently ranked lowest in the aforementioned indicators, highlighting the superior efficacy of the combined treatment approach. As for IAR, no significant difference was observed among the interventions. Consequently, the integration of CPMs in combination therapies could enhance efficacy while maintaining safety. Based on the results of this study, each combination therapy involving CPMs had its advantages and disadvantages. WS+T/Q ranked first, second and first in improving CUHR, ER and reducing RPUR, respectively, might exhibit superior efficacy. However, WS+T/Q ranked last with the highest IAR among the interventions, indicating a potential safety concern. AWY+T/Q and PYHW+T/Q showed less favourable safety profiles because they ranked fifth and sixth. The efficacy of WFC+T/Q and JHWK+T/Q was less than satisfactory due to their ranks in improving CUHR. Overall, none of the combination therapies were deemed completely satisfactory. Cluster analysis was used to further assess the rankings of the interventions. JWYY+T/Q was the best treatment strategy among the interventions considering the safety (IAR) and efficacy (CUHR, ER and HP ER), followed by a cluster including KFX+T/Q. Simultaneously, the optimal bunch with lower RPUR and IAR also encompassed KFX+T/Q. Therefore, JWYY+T/Q might be deemed the most advantageous choice, followed by KFX+T/Q. An NMA 66 of Chinese herbal formulae for HP -positive PUD showed that the combination therapies involving TCMs held clinical significance. These Chinese herbal formulas included three CPMs such as JHWK, KFX and WFC. The results of this NMA showed that combination therapy with KFX could be the superior option among these combination therapies with CPMs, aligning with the results of our study. Several studies have been undertaken to investigate the underlying mechanisms for CPMs against PUD. It is known that JWYY has inhibitory effects on gastric acid secretion and pepsin activity 67 and could improve gastrointestinal mucosa surface hydrophobicity and mucous gel layer stability, 68–70 thereby inhibiting mucosal damage. In addition, JWYY could stimulate angiogenesis and promote mucosal regeneration by increasing platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor. 71 72 KFX can inhibit inflammation and oxidative stress by reducing the expression of inflammatory factors and thus inhibit mucosal damage. 73–75 KFX could also stimulate angiogenesis, promote mucosal regeneration and enhance growth factor expression. 73–75 Taken together, JWYY and KFX demonstrated strong efficacy in preventing mucosal injury, enhancing defence mechanisms in the gastrointestinal mucosa and promoting mucosal repair. These studies and findings provided strong evidence to support our research. Numerous combination therapies with CPMs have been reported to be available for treating PUD patients with HP . However, there is a lack of direct evidence comparing these combined therapies. As the first NMA to compare seven combination therapies with CPMs and T/Q, our study provided valuable insight for selecting the appropriate treatment option. Nevertheless, some limitations need to be improved. First, the quality of the included studies was unsatisfactory. Although all the studies included were RCTs, 24 of them failed to appropriately describe the methods of random allocation. Additionally, none of the included studies mentioned allocation concealment or blinding methods. IAR might, therefore, be affected in the RCTs. Second, the rapid urease test or the test performed within a timeframe of less than 4 weeks postcessation of medication may yield false-negative outcomes, rendering it unsuitable for evaluating HP eradication. 2 3 The data pertaining to HP ER from certain RCTs 29 39 41–44 46 47 54 55 59–61 63 were excluded, influencing the overall analysis due to the relative sample size. Consequently, it is advisable to carefully choose an appropriate detection method to ascertain the recurrence of PUD. 2 4 18 Third, the RPUR was reported in only 12 of the 36 included RCTs, potentially impacting the accuracy of our findings. Fourth, it was known that factors such as patients’ age, current smoking and/or drinking habits, the locations and sizes of ulcers, antibiotic resistance of HP , various T/Q therapy regimens and recent use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) could be identified as the effect modifiers. 76–78 Baseline comparisons between arms revealed no significant differences in patients’ ages or the locations and sizes of ulcers (see online supplemental table S2 ). However, variations in antibiotic regimens and the duration of therapeutic courses could potentially introduce heterogeneity. Furthermore, current smoking and/or drinking habits, antibiotic resistance of HP and recent use of NSAIDs were not addressed in the included studies. In light of potential heterogeneity, heterogeneity tests were performed for each outcome in this NMA. It is known that the prediction interval can tell us how much the effect size varies and can be used to evaluate the impact of effect measure modification. 79 In the absence of between-study heterogeneity, the prediction interval coincides with the respective CI. 25 Within this NMA, the heterogeneity test results showed that only 8 of 84 comparisons involving 5 outcomes, including 3 of the 28 comparisons involving CUHR, 3 of the 15 comparisons involving ER and 2 of the 10 comparisons involving HP ER, were influenced by estimated heterogeneity, while the comparisons involving RPUR and IAR were not influenced by estimated heterogeneity. Therefore, we contended that most of the results of the comparisons among the interventions in this NMA were stable and reliable, as evidenced by the prediction interval data. It should be noted, however, that the precision of the prediction interval may be compromised by the limited number of studies included. The seven combination therapies with CPMs have been extensively used in clinical settings due to their safety and proven efficacy. Moving forward, more high-quality RCTs would be included to improve the reliability and stability of NMA by providing more robust outcome indicators. Conclusions JWYY+T/Q might be the most favourable option for HP -positive PUD among the seven combination therapies with the CPMs, followed by KFX+T/Q. However, this finding should be interpreted with caution due to the limited available evidence. Further high-quality RCTs are necessary to assess the effectiveness and safety of these CPMs in managing HP -positive PUD. documents.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy may help improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes (such as fewer preterm birth and low birthweight babies) and reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes (such as severe postpartum haemorrhage).
OBJECTIVES: To examine whether vitamin D supplementation alone or in combination with calcium or other vitamins and minerals given to women during pregnancy can safely improve certain maternal and neonatal outcomes.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register (which includes results of comprehensive searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and relevant conference proceedings) (3 December 2022). We also searched the reference lists of retrieved studies.
SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised and quasi-randomised trials evaluating the effect of supplementation with vitamin D alone or in combination with other micronutrients for women during pregnancy in comparison to placebo or no intervention.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors independently i) assessed the eligibility of studies against the inclusion criteria, ii) assessed trustworthiness based on pre-defined criteria of scientific integrity, iii) extracted data from included studies, and iv) assessed the risk of bias of the included studies. We assessed the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach.
MAIN RESULTS: The previous version of this review included 30 studies; in this update, we have removed 20 of these studies to 'awaiting classification' following assessments of trustworthiness, one study has been excluded, and one new study included. This current review has a total of 10 included studies, 117 excluded studies, 34 studies in awaiting assessment, and seven ongoing studies. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence. This removal of the studies resulted in evidence that was downgraded to low-certainty or very low-certainty due to study design limitations, inconsistency between studies, and imprecision. Supplementation with vitamin D compared to no intervention or a placebo A total of eight studies involving 2313 pregnant women were included in this comparison. We assessed four studies as having a low risk of bias for most domains and four studies as having high risk or unclear risk of bias for most domains. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D during pregnancy compared to placebo or no intervention on pre-eclampsia (risk ratio (RR) 0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.21 to 1.33; 1 study, 165 women), gestational diabetes (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.03 to 8.28; 1 study, 165 women), preterm birth (< 37 weeks) (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.33; 3 studies, 1368 women), nephritic syndrome (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.06; 1 study, 135 women), or hypercalcaemia (1 study; no cases reported). Supplementation with vitamin D during pregnancy may reduce the risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage; however, only one study reported this outcome (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.91; 1 study, 1134 women; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce the risk of low birthweight; however, the upper CI suggests that an increase in risk cannot be ruled out (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.08; 3 studies, 371 infants; low-certainty evidence). Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium compared to no intervention or a placebo One study involving 84 pregnant women was included in this comparison. Overall, this study was at moderate to high risk of bias. Pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and maternal adverse events were not reported. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D and calcium on preterm birth (RR not estimable; very low-certainty evidence) or for low birthweight (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.14 to 14.94; very low-certainty evidence) compared to women who received placebo or no intervention. Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium + other vitamins and minerals versus calcium + other vitamins and minerals (but no vitamin D) One study involving 1298 pregnant women was included in this comparison. We assessed this study as having a low risk of bias in all domains. Pre-eclampsia was not reported. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of supplementation with vitamin D, calcium, and other vitamins and minerals during pregnancy compared to no vitamin D on gestational diabetes (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.73; very low-certainty evidence), maternal adverse events (hypercalcaemia no events and hypercalciuria RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.02 to 3.97; very low-certainty evidence), preterm birth (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), or low birthweight (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.51; low-certainty evidence).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: This updated review using the trustworthy assessment tool removed 21 studies from the previous update and added one new study for a total of 10 included studies. In this setting, supplementation with vitamin D alone compared to no intervention or a placebo resulted in very uncertain evidence on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, or nephritic syndrome. It may reduce the risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage; however, only one study reported this outcome. It may also reduce the risk of low birthweight; however, the upper CI suggests that an increase in risk cannot be ruled out. Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium versus placebo or no intervention resulted in very uncertain evidence on preterm birth and low birthweight. Pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and maternal adverse events were not reported in the only study included in this comparison. Supplementation with vitamin D + calcium + other vitamins and minerals versus calcium + other vitamins and minerals (but no vitamin D) resulted in very uncertain evidence on gestational diabetes and maternal adverse events (hypercalciuria) and uncertain evidence on preterm birth and low birthweight. Pre-eclampsia was not reported in the only study included in this comparison. All findings warrant further research. Additional rigorous, high-quality, and larger randomised trials are required to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation in pregnancy, particularly in relation to the risk of maternal adverse events.
